license.payload: Per item, recorded in origin.items. Nikola Tesla died in 1943; every work here was published between 1888 and 1919 and is in the public domain in the United States (published before 1931), and the author's term of life plus seventy years has run everywhere it applies. The United States patents are federal government publications, with no copyright. The Electrical Experimenter issues of February–June 1919 are University of Toronto copies with no licence stated at the item; the October 1919 issue is marked Public Domain Mark 1.0 at the item. The Century issue is a microfilm copy with no licence stated at the item. The AIEE Transactions volume is a microfilm copy with no licence stated at the item. The two Google scans are marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT at the item. Wikisource pages are CC BY-SA 4.0 for the site's contributions; Project Gutenberg texts are under the Project Gutenberg licence, carried in each file.

normalization: Originals as fetched under original/: Internet Archive scans and OCR layers, Wikisource HTML as served with its revision id, Project Gutenberg plain text as served. text/<slug>.ocr.txt is the Archive's OCR with line endings normalized; text/<slug>.txt is the Wikisource parser output reduced by code, or the Gutenberg file with line endings normalized. Five magazine issues and one volume of Transactions are held by reference (identifier, file, size and md5), their OCR layers copied. No text was corrected by hand.
scope: Tesla's own account of his work and the texts on which his reputation was made. My Inventions is held twice: in the six issues of the Electrical Experimenter where it first appeared (February, March, April, May, June and October 1919), and in the Wikisource transcription. The 1891 lecture at Columbia College is held in its first printing, Transactions of the AIEE 8 (1891), and in Martin's collection of 1894. The 1892 London lecture is held in the Johnston book of 1892 and in Gutenberg's text of it. Martin's Inventions, Researches and Writings (1894) also carries the 1888 AIEE paper on the polyphase system and the 1893 lecture On Light and Other High Frequency Phenomena; it is held as a scan with OCR and as Gutenberg's text. “The Problem of Increasing Human Energy” is held in the Century issue of June 1900 and in the Wikisource transcription. Twelve United States patents are held as the printed specifications. They were chosen to follow the line of the work: the polyphase system of 1888 (381,968 the induction motor, 382,280 the transmission system, 382,282 the transformers); the high-frequency work of 1891 (454,622 the resonant transformer, 462,418 the disruptive-discharge circuit); telautomatics (613,809, 1898); wireless transmission and radio (645,576 and 649,621, 1900; 685,958, 1901; 787,412, 1905); the turbine (1,061,206, 1913); and the Wardenclyffe transmitter (1,119,732, 1914). US 382,845, named in the brief beside the coil, is a commutator for dynamo-electric machines (15 May 1888); the coil is 454,622. The other ninety-odd patents on the Archive are left on the shelf there, and the Colorado Springs notes (1899–1900, first printed 1978) are not seated: their first publication is too late for the public domain in the United States.

why_seated: Tesla is the inventor who wrote down the method of invention: the device built and run in the mind before it is built in the shop, and the account in My Inventions of a mind that took itself for an automaton responding to impressions. The seat holds that account beside the patents and lectures it narrates, so the claim and the specification can be read against each other. It answers the operator's call for the exact sciences at EA-CORPORA-30.
ruling: Lee Sharks, 2026-10-30: “and then an ea-corpora seating... Einstein, Gödel, Tesla, Copernicus, Galileo, classical Arabic mathematicians... what is in the public domain, and what else? and just to be perverse lets seat the promised Klee notebooks with them”; to the proposed set: “yes, thats a good set”.
